Photo location guide

Add Location to Photos on Mac: Manual and Batch

Use the Info window for a known place, a Smart Album to find missing GPS, and time matching when one trip contains many different locations.

Updated November 4, 2026

Add a location with the Photos Info windowFind missing GPS with a Smart AlbumChoose a method for each groupCheck capture times before matching a tripUse LensPin for Mac as the batch optionDecide whether you also need a GPS-bearing file

Add a location with the Photos Info window

  1. Open Photos on your Mac and select a photo. Press Command-I or click the Info button.
  2. Enter a place in the location field and select the matching result.
  3. Check the map and nearby landmarks. If the place is wrong, search again or adjust the pin.
  4. Close and reopen the information for that photo to confirm the place you intended is there.

You can select several photos before using Info when they all belong at one location. Keep the selection narrow: a meal at one restaurant is different from a day that includes a drive and several stops. Apple explains these controls in its Photos metadata guide.

For a shared location, another built-in option is Image > Location > Copy Location on the reference photo, then Image > Location > Assign Location on the selected targets. Verify that you selected only the intended photos. A copied location has no understanding of how far you walked between shots.

Find missing GPS with a Smart Album

A Smart Album gives you a working list without moving files around. Choose File > New Smart Album, name it something like “Missing location,” and set the condition to Photo / is not / tagged with GPS. The menus can vary by Photos version; look for the equivalent GPS condition. Start with this single rule before adding date or camera filters.

Apple’s Smart Album guide explains how conditions work. You can later narrow the album to a trip by adding a date condition and requiring all conditions to match. Smart Albums created on Mac do not appear as Smart Albums on iPhone or iPad.

Use the list as a queue, then inspect individual photos. Screenshots and other images may be intentionally without GPS, so there is no need to fill every item. A photo that disappears from a missing-GPS album after editing should still be checked in Info; leaving the queue alone does not prove that its new place is correct.

Choose a method for each group

If you remember one venue, use the manual method. If you have a real timed route, use the GPX workflow on Mac. If you took iPhone photos along the way, use those as clues for a batch. These choices depend on the clues you retained, rather than the camera brand.

For an old trip, split the job into places you know, periods covered by references, and periods you cannot reconstruct confidently. Keep uncertain photos unassigned until you have better information. A city center pin can be a conscious approximation, but should not be mistaken for a recovered shooting position.

Check capture times before matching a trip

Compare the recorded times of a camera photo and a geotagged (with a saved location) reference showing the same moment. Check the date as well as the hour, especially after flights or around midnight. A camera left in another time zone can create a consistent offset; clocks changed during a trip require separate attention.

Do not change every photo’s date just to make a map suggestion look right. First establish the actual clock difference using more than one recognizable moment. Separate cameras may have separate offsets. A good match near breakfast is not enough clues for a second camera’s evening images.

Use LensPin for Mac as the batch option

LensPin has a native Mac app requiring macOS 14+. Photos need to be in the Apple Photos library first; LensPin does not import from a camera. It matches their capture times against geotagged iPhone photos from the same trip, geotagged photos from other cameras, GPX (a route file with times and coordinates) tracks or Apple Health/Fitness workout routes. It does not record GPX.

  1. Start with one trip’s photos that have no location. Journeys are grouped automatically, but still check the time period you are working on.
  2. Choose available location clues and inspect whether it covers the photographs’ times.
  3. Preview a camera clock offset if needed. The preview does not change capture dates.
  4. Review every suggestion before saving. Check stops, route changes and gaps carefully; skip unsupported positions.
  5. Return to Photos, open Info for saved items, and compare their places with the trip you remember.

Processing happens on device. Existing locations are never overwritten, so a photo that already has the wrong location needs attention in Apple Photos rather than an expectation that batch filling will replace it. See the map diagnosis guide if the location is present but the map still seems wrong.

Decide whether you also need a GPS-bearing file

Saving in LensPin updates the Apple Photos library, not original files in your camera backup or Finder folders. To produce a separate image with GPS in EXIF, export a JPG copy and enable Include location. Open that exported copy to verify it before handing it to someone else. Keep location disabled when sharing a place you want private.

Free download. The first 100 photos/videos located are free. Saving a location to one photo or video counts as one use; skipped and failed items do not count. After that, LensPin Unlimited is an optional one-time purchase, with no subscription. See the App Store for the price in your region.
